 Why isn’t Angel Reese held to the Caitlin Clark standard when fans attack her teammates?
 Tuesday, 3 November 2026, 23:38 
 Photo source: Fox News 
 Commentators have repeatedly pressed Caitlin Clark to answer for online abuse. But as Jordin Canada and Rhyne Howard face attacks from people identifying as Angel Reese fans, the article asks why Reese is not being held to the same standard. 
 Atlanta Dream players Jordin Canada and Rhyne Howard have faced online attacks from people claiming to support Angel Reese. Some posts accused Howard, coach Karl Smesko and the Dream’s owners of selling Reese out in a supposedly rigged Finals. Others called Canada and Howard “BOTH selfish players and human beings” and accused them of not caring about winning. Some posts also contained racist language, including the N-word.
 This is reported by Fox News .
 The article contrasts the response with the repeated demands that Caitlin Clark condemn online hate directed at others. Clark has condemned such abuse several times. On July 3, she spoke about harassment of opponents, teammates and coaches.
 The harassment, the hate, none of that is okay. 
 – Caitlin Clark
 At her October 8 season-ending news conference, Clark was asked about Kelsey Mitchell’s comments on the treatment she receives and the attention the team gets because of Clark. She said she opposed people using her to promote racist rhetoric, hate or discrimination. On October 23, ESPN analyst Monica McNutt said:
 There is no way that someone would use my likeness to support causes that I am against. 
 – Monica McNutt
 The article asks whether McNutt and other commentators will make similar demands of Reese. So far, it says, the WNBA media has not done so. Canada returned to social media after avoiding it during the playoffs and wrote:
 It blows my mind that as fans yall CHOOSE to say the hurtful and cruel things out loud and on here 
 – Jordin Canada
 Meanwhile, Reese said in a post on her private secondary Instagram account that she was pausing her podcast for the offseason, planned occasional YouTube vlogs and would spend time resting and working out in Florida. She wrote:
 i’m dedicating this off season to myself. 
 – Angel Reese
 The writer argues that if Clark announced a six-month break to focus on herself while teammates received abusive messages, commentators would likely question her leadership and accountability. The article asks why they are not applying that scrutiny to Reese, while maintaining that neither player owes anyone a statement.
 Advertisement 
 The article also points to the league’s attention to online abuse. In August, after Sophie Cunningham’s comments about “biological men” competing in women’s sports prompted an eligibility debate, Commissioner Cathy Engelbert told teams an upcoming meeting of the WNBA’s anti-hate task force would address whether males should be eligible to play. Yahoo Sports reported that the meeting instead focused largely on online hate directed at players.
 At an October 17 press conference before Game 1 of the WNBA Finals, Engelbert condemned people who sit “behind a keyboard to spew vitriol and hate and racism and misogyny at our players.” The writer says they were not called on to ask why online commentary receives so much attention from the league. The article concludes that commentators who have assigned Clark responsibility for online abuse should explain why they do not apply the same standard when Reese’s teammates are targeted.
